subsection: 5. Factors affecting the absorption of minerals

notes.h: How iron is absorbed and stored (assumed knowledge)
points: Most iron is absorbed in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Absorbed iron binds to transferrin, a protein that carries it in the blood to where it is needed.
Surplus iron is stored in the liver as ferritin, and the body has little ability to excrete iron.
Iron is lost in small amounts through sweat, shed skin cells and, in women, menstrual blood.

notes.h: The role of vitamins in iron and calcium absorption
points: Vitamin C converts non-haem iron from the ferric form (Fe³⁺) to the ferrous form (Fe²⁺), which is absorbed more readily.
Vitamin C also aids the absorption of calcium.
Vitamin D stimulates the production of a calcium-binding protein in the lining of the small intestine, increasing calcium absorption.
Vitamin D increases the absorption of phosphorus, which must be present in a balanced ratio with calcium.
Where vitamin D is lacking, calcium absorption falls even when dietary calcium is adequate, so bones weaken.
Haem iron comes from animal foods such as red meat, liver, poultry and fish, and is already in the ferrous form.
Haem iron is absorbed more readily than non-haem iron, and its absorption is largely unaffected by other foods in the meal.
Non-haem iron comes from plant foods, pulses, wholegrain cereals, nuts, seeds, dark green vegetables and eggs.
Non-haem iron is in the ferric form and must be converted to the ferrous form before the intestine can absorb it.
Eating meat, fish or poultry in the same meal as non-haem iron foods increases the absorption of non-haem iron, an effect known as the meat factor.
Vitamin C is a major enhancer of non-haem iron absorption, acting on the ferric iron in plant foods.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps convert ferric iron to ferrous iron, aiding absorption.
Eating vitamin C-rich fruit or vegetables with an iron-rich meal increases absorption, for example a glass of orange juice with lentils.
Tannins in tea and coffee bind iron into an insoluble compound, so these drinks should not be taken with an iron-rich meal.
Phytates in wholegrain cereals and pulses bind iron and reduce its absorption.
Oxalates in spinach and rhubarb bind iron, reducing its absorption.
Calcium from dairy products or supplements taken with a meal competes with iron for absorption.
Vitamin D is the main vitamin that drives calcium absorption from the intestine.
Lactose, the sugar in milk, improves calcium absorption.
An acidic environment in the stomach and small intestine keeps calcium soluble and easier to absorb.
Adequate protein provides amino acids that combine with calcium to make it more soluble, aiding absorption.
Parathormone, the parathyroid hormone, raises blood calcium by increasing its absorption from food and its release from bone.
Oestrogen supports calcium absorption and bone retention, and the fall in oestrogen after menopause increases the risk of osteoporosis.

notes.h: Other factors that inhibit calcium absorption
points: Excess dietary fibre reduces calcium absorption.
Excess fat in the diet reduces calcium absorption by binding to it in the intestine.
Caffeine in tea and coffee increases the loss of calcium in urine.
Excess salt increases the loss of calcium in urine.
Alcohol reduces calcium absorption and increases its loss from the body.
Smoking and nicotine reduce calcium absorption and bone density.

notes.h: Phytates and oxalates and calcium absorption (Higher Level only)
points: Phytic acid, found in cereal grains, bran and pulses, binds calcium to form calcium phytate, an insoluble compound that the body cannot absorb.
Oxalic acid, found in spinach and rhubarb, binds calcium to form calcium oxalate, which is insoluble and not absorbed.
Because of its oxalate, the calcium in spinach is poorly absorbed, even though spinach contains calcium.
Phytates and oxalates are most damaging when eaten in large amounts at the same meal as calcium-rich foods such as milk or cheese.

keyTerms.definition: Iron from animal foods that is already in the ferrous form and is absorbed readily, largely independent of other foods in the meal.
Iron from plant foods and eggs, in the ferric form, which must be converted to the ferrous form before it is absorbed.
The Fe²⁺ form of iron, which the intestine absorbs more readily than the ferric form.
The Fe³⁺ form of iron, which is less readily absorbed and must be reduced by vitamin C or stomach acid.
A compound in cereal grains, bran and pulses that binds iron and calcium into insoluble forms the body cannot absorb.
A compound in spinach and rhubarb that binds calcium and iron into insoluble forms the body cannot absorb.
Compounds in tea and coffee that bind iron and reduce its absorption when the drinks are taken with food.
The effect by which meat, fish or poultry eaten with plant foods increases the absorption of non-haem iron.
The parathyroid hormone that raises blood calcium by increasing absorption from food and release from bone.
The protein in the liver that stores surplus iron until the body needs it.

questions.prompt: Explain how vitamin C increases the absorption of iron from a vegetarian meal.
questions.model: Non-haem iron from plant foods is in the ferric (Fe³⁺) form, which is poorly absorbed. Vitamin C reduces it to the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form, which the small intestine absorbs more readily. Vitamin C also helps by creating an acidic environment that aids iron absorption. Example from a vegetarian meal: a salad of spinach, tomato and red pepper with lemon juice dressing. One mark each for the ferric to ferrous conversion, the greater absorption of ferrous iron, and a correct example of vitamin C in the meal.

questions.prompt: Discuss the factors that aid and inhibit the absorption of calcium and iron from food, and explain how these factors could affect the planning of a diet.
questions.model: Iron: haem iron from meat, fish and poultry is absorbed readily; non-haem iron from plant foods and eggs must be converted from ferric to ferrous form. Aids: vitamin C, meat, fish or poultry eaten at the same meal (the meat factor), stomach acid. Inhibitors: tannins in tea and coffee, phytates in wholegrain cereals and pulses, oxalates in spinach and rhubarb, calcium taken at the same meal. Calcium: aided by vitamin D, lactose, an acidic environment, adequate protein and parathormone; oestrogen supports retention. Inhibitors: excess fibre, excess fat, caffeine, excess salt, alcohol, smoking; phytic and oxalic acids bind calcium into insoluble forms. Diet planning: pair non-haem iron foods with vitamin C sources and avoid tea or coffee at iron-rich meals; include vitamin D sources; use dairy or fortified foods for calcium while limiting excess salt, caffeine and alcohol; make sure spinach and rhubarb are not counted as reliable calcium sources.
